sections.title: Part IV Overview (stub)
sections.summary: A short (printed IV-3 to IV-11, pdf_page ~336-346) state-of-the-knowledge summary on mechanistic-empirical (M-E) pavement design concepts, NOT incorporated into the Guide's actual design procedures (Parts II-III remain empirical, AASHO-Road-Test-based). Explicitly out of scope for this module per the build brief; stub only.
sections.body: Part IV explains that while a considerable body of mechanistic-model information exists, the Task Force believed significant improvements would occur as these models are calibrated to in-service performance and incorporated into everyday design usage -- but had not, as of 1993, been incorporated into the Guide's actual (Part II/III) design procedures. Topics covered at a conceptual level: an example M-E model development framework (Figure 1.1: traffic/subgrade/environment/material inputs -> trial thicknesses -> structural analysis -> distress analysis across multiple distress modes (fatigue cracking, rutting, thermal cracking, frost effects, reflection cracking, faulting, punchout, roughness) -> calibrated distress predictions -> life-cycle prediction/cost, feeding both initial design and rehabilitation methodology), benefits of M-E approaches, a framework for development/application, and implementation considerations (design considerations, input data, equipment acquisition, computer hardware/software, training, field testing/calibration).
key_points: State-of-the-knowledge summary; NOT incorporated into the Guide's actual (empirical) design procedures
Figure 1.1: conceptual M-E design/rehabilitation framework diagram (inputs -> structural analysis -> multi-mode distress analysis -> calibrated predictions -> life-cycle cost)
Distress modes addressed conceptually: fatigue cracking, rutting, thermal cracking, frost effects, reflection cracking, faulting, punchout, roughness
Implementation topics: design considerations, input data, equipment, computer hardware/software, training, field testing/calibration
